nodes.title: Economic Growth and Its Measurement: GDP, GNP, NNP Etc
prelimsNote: GDP = market value of final goods & services produced within the domestic territory; GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad; NNP = GNP − depreciation.
National Income = NNP at factor cost; market price = factor cost + net indirect taxes (indirect taxes − subsidies).
GVA at basic prices + product taxes − product subsidies = GDP; India adopted GVA with the 2011-12 base revision (2015).
GDP deflator = nominal GDP ÷ real GDP × 100 — covers all goods and services, broader than CPI/WPI.
Trap: national income is the money value of FINAL goods & services (UPSC 2013); intermediate goods excluded to avoid double counting.
PPP: India is the 3rd largest economy by PPP — the UPSC 2019 statement saying 'sixth' was false.

nodes.title: Inclusive Growth — Concept, Strategies & India's Record
prelimsNote: 11th Plan theme 'faster and more inclusive growth'; 12th Plan 'faster, more inclusive and sustainable growth'.
Instruments (UPSC 2011): skill development, financial inclusion, rural infrastructure, social-sector spending.
Inclusive governance (UPSC 2012): effective District Planning Committees, more public health spending, Mid-day Meal — NOT allowing NBFCs to do banking.
Measured through poverty, inequality (Gini), employment quality and regional disparity — growth can occur without development (UPSC 2018).
Inclusive growth targets broad-based gains in income, jobs and access to services for the bottom of the distribution — not just higher average growth.

nodes.title: Indian Economy at Independence — Challenges & Choices
prelimsNote: Colonial legacy: stagnant agriculture, de-industrialisation, drain of wealth (Dadabhai Naoroji, 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India').
Pre-independence plans: Bombay Plan 1944 (industrialists), Gandhian Plan (S.N. Agarwal), People's Plan (M.N. Roy), Sarvodaya Plan (J.P. Narayan).
Planning Commission set up in March 1950 by a Cabinet resolution — non-constitutional, non-statutory; National Development Council set up in 1952.
Industrial Policy Resolutions 1948 and 1956 shaped the mixed economy with public sector at the 'commanding heights'.
First Five-Year Plan (1951–56) used the Harrod–Domar model with focus on agriculture and irrigation.

nodes.title: Five Year Plans — Objectives, Phases & NITI Aayog
prelimsNote: 2nd Plan (1956–61): Mahalanobis model, heavy industry — determined thrust on basic & capital goods (UPSC 2019); 3rd Plan failure led to Plan Holidays (1966–69).
4th Plan (1969–74): growth with stability, aimed to correct concentration of wealth and economic power (UPSC 2019); 5th Plan: 'Garibi Hatao', terminated in 1978 (Rolling Plans 1978–80).
8th Plan (1992–97): indicative planning after LPG reforms; 11th Plan: 'Faster and more inclusive growth'; 12th Plan (2012–17): 'Faster, More Inclusive and Sustainable Growth' (UPSC 2014).
NITI Aayog: 1 Jan 2015 by Cabinet resolution — neither constitutional nor statutory; PM chairperson; Governing Council of all CMs and LGs.
NITI is a think tank — no power to allocate funds to States (unlike the Planning Commission); hosts the Atal Innovation Mission (UPSC 2019).
Trap: the 5th Plan did NOT first make the financial sector an integral part of the Plan (UPSC 2019 statement 3 was false).

nodes.title: Nehruvian Socialist Economy vs Liberalisation
prelimsNote: Nehruvian model: Mahalanobis heavy-industry strategy, public sector at 'commanding heights', import substitution, licence-permit raj.
Controls: MRTP Act 1969, FERA 1973 (replaced by FEMA 1999); 14 banks nationalised in 1969, 6 more in 1980.
'Hindu rate of growth' (Raj Krishna) ≈ 3.5% a year during 1950–80.
1991 BoP crisis: forex reserves covered barely two to three weeks of imports; gold pledged with the Bank of England and Bank of Japan.
Shift to LPG (liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation) in July 1991 under PM P.V. Narasimha Rao and FM Manmohan Singh.

nodes.title: Employment
prelimsNote: Types: disguised (marginal productivity of labour ≈ zero, typical of agriculture), structural (mismatch between job vacancies and worker skills/location), frictional (between jobs), cyclical (recession-driven), seasonal.
PLFS by NSO (since 2017-18) replaced NSSO employment–unemployment rounds; measures Usual Status (principal + subsidiary) and Current Weekly Status.
Key ratios: LFPR = labour force ÷ population; Worker Population Ratio = employed ÷ population; Unemployment Rate = unemployed ÷ labour force.
Labour Bureau (Ministry of Labour) compiles data on industrial disputes, closures, retrenchments and lay-offs (UPSC 2022).
Four Labour Codes (Wages 2019; Industrial Relations, Social Security, OSH 2020) consolidate 29 central labour laws.
Trap: fixed-term employment under the Standing Orders amendment (2018) made hiring/lay-off easier (UPSC 2019); not all casual workers get EPF cover (UPSC 2021).

nodes.title: Banking Sector — NPA Crisis, Recapitalisation & Reforms
prelimsNote: NPA: interest or principal overdue for more than 90 days; Asset Quality Review (2015) exposed hidden stress.
Resolution tools: DRTs (1993), SARFAESI Act 2002, ARCs, IBC 2016; Inter-Creditor Agreement (2019) for faster resolution of stressed assets ≥ ₹50 crore under consortium lending (UPSC 2019).
Recapitalisation bonds (2017); Indradhanush (2015) created the Banks Board Bureau; PSB mergers reduced their number from 27 to 12 (2017–2020).
Prompt Corrective Action framework triggers on capital, asset quality and leverage thresholds.
Interest Coverage Ratio = EBIT ÷ interest — a higher ratio means better ability to service debt (UPSC 2020).
Banks Board Bureau recommends heads of PSBs and helps them with strategies and capital-raising plans; the RBI Governor is NOT its chairman (UPSC 2019, 2022).

nodes.title: Bad Bank (NARCL) — Concept & Implementation
prelimsNote: National Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd (NARCL) announced in Budget 2021; licensed by RBI as an ARC under SARFAESI; majority-owned by PSBs.
India Debt Resolution Company Ltd (IDRCL) manages and resolves the acquired assets (majority private ownership).
Structure: 15% cash and 85% Security Receipts, backed by a Government guarantee of up to ₹30,600 crore.
Targets large NPAs of ₹500 crore and above.

nodes.title: Financial Inclusion — Jan Dhan, Payment Banks & Digital Finance
prelimsNote: PMJDY (Aug 2014): zero-balance accounts, RuPay debit card with accident cover, overdraft up to ₹10,000 (UPSC 2015).
Payments Banks (Nachiket Mor Committee): accept deposits up to ₹2 lakh, cannot lend or issue credit cards (UPSC 2016).
Small Finance Banks: 75% of credit to priority sectors; at least 50% of loans up to ₹25 lakh (UPSC 2017).
Business Correspondents (2006), Lead Bank Scheme (1969), Service Area Approach (1989, under the Lead Bank Scheme — UPSC 2019).
RBI's Financial Inclusion Index (since 2021) measures access, usage and quality.

nodes.title: NBFC Sector — Shadow Banking & Regulation
prelimsNote: NBFCs are registered under the Companies Act and regulated by RBI (Chapter IIIB, RBI Act).
Unlike banks: cannot accept demand deposits, are not part of the payment & settlement system, cannot issue cheques drawn on themselves; no DICGC deposit insurance.
Scale-Based Regulation (2021): base, middle, upper and top layers.
Not all NBFC-like entities are RBI-regulated: insurance (IRDAI), stock-broking/mutual funds (SEBI), chit funds (State governments), Nidhi companies (MCA).
IL&FS default (2018) exposed shadow-banking contagion risk.

nodes.title: Insolvency & Bankruptcy Code (IBC) — Framework & Cases
prelimsNote: IBC 2016; Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) is the regulator.
Adjudicating authority: NCLT for companies/LLPs, DRT for individuals/partnerships; appeals to NCLAT, then the Supreme Court.
CIRP: 180 days + 90-day extension; 330-day outer limit including litigation (2019 amendment).
Committee of Creditors decides with 66% vote; its commercial wisdom has primacy (Essar Steel 2019).
Sec 29A bars defaulting promoters from bidding; pre-packaged insolvency for MSMEs (2021); minimum default threshold ₹1 crore (2020).

nodes.title: Digital Payments — UPI, BHIM & Fintech Ecosystem
prelimsNote: NPCI (2008): not-for-profit company promoted by banks under the RBI's Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007 framework.
NPCI runs NFS (links all ATMs — UPSC 2018), RuPay, UPI (2016), BHIM, IMPS, AePS, NETC FASTag and Bharat BillPay (UPSC 2017).
Merchant Discount Rate = fee charged to merchants by banks for accepting card payments (UPSC 2018); MDR set to zero for RuPay debit and BHIM-UPI from 2020.
RBI's 2018 data-localisation directive: all payment-system data must be stored only in India (UPSC 2019).
CBDC (e₹) pilots from Nov–Dec 2022; programmable features possible, payments without SWIFT (UPSC 2023).

nodes.title: RBI — Monetary Policy, Inflation Targeting & MPC
prelimsNote: Flexible inflation targeting under the amended RBI Act (2016) and the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement (2015): CPI-Combined 4% ± 2%, set by the Government every five years.
MPC: 6 members — Governor (casting vote), Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one RBI officer, and 3 external members appointed by the Government for 4 years; meets at least 4 times a year.
If inflation stays outside the band for 3 consecutive quarters, RBI must report reasons and remedial action to the Government.
Corridor: Standing Deposit Facility (floor, since April 2022) < repo rate < MSF (ceiling, repo + 25 bps); Bank Rate is aligned with MSF.
Stances: accommodative, neutral, withdrawal of accommodation, calibrated tightening.
Trap: RBI draws its powers from the RBI Act 1934, and Government directions come under Sec 7 of that Act — not from the Constitution (UPSC 2021).

nodes.title: Capital Markets — SEBI Regulation, Bond Market & Corporate Governance
prelimsNote: SEBI set up in 1988, statutory under the SEBI Act 1992; appeals go to the Securities Appellate Tribunal.
SEBI regulates stock exchanges, mutual funds, credit rating agencies (not RBI — UPSC 2022), REITs/InvITs and Alternative Investment Funds.
Primary market (new issues/IPOs) vs secondary market (trading); T+1 settlement cycle adopted in 2023.
CSR under Sec 135, Companies Act 2013: 2% of average net profit for companies above thresholds.
Corporate bond market is shallow; G-secs dominate debt markets.

nodes.title: Venture Capital & Start-up Funding Ecosystem
prelimsNote: Venture capital = short-to-medium-term risk capital for new/early-stage ventures (UPSC 2014).
SEBI AIF Regulations 2012: Category I (VC funds, angel funds, SME, social venture, infrastructure), Category II (PE, debt funds), Category III (hedge funds).
Fund of Funds for Startups (SIDBI) invests in SEBI-registered AIFs.
Angel investors fund the earliest stage; 'angel tax' abolished from FY 2025-26.

nodes.title: Government Budgeting — Types, Outcome Budget & Process
prelimsNote: Art 112 'Annual Financial Statement' — the word 'Budget' is not in the Constitution; charged expenditure is not voted on.
Art 266(1) Consolidated Fund (appropriation needed), Art 266(2) Public Account (no appropriation), Art 267 Contingency Fund (at the President's disposal).
Reforms: Outcome Budget (2005), Gender Budgeting (2005-06), Budget date moved to 1 February and Railway Budget merged (2017), plan/non-plan distinction removed (2017-18).
Vote on account (Art 116) covers only expenditure; an interim budget covers receipts and expenditure (UPSC 2011).
FRBM-mandated documents: Macro-economic Framework Statement and Medium-term Fiscal Policy cum Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement (UPSC 2020).
Capital budget includes loans to States, recovery of loans, disinvestment and investment in PSUs (UPSC 2016).

nodes.title: Fiscal Deficit — FRBM Act, Targets & Fiscal Consolidation
prelimsNote: Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts) = total borrowing requirement.
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments; Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts; Effective revenue deficit = revenue deficit − grants for creation of capital assets.
Monetised deficit = RBI's net credit to the Centre; FRBM barred RBI from subscribing to primary G-sec issues from 2006 (only Ways & Means Advances).
FRBM Act 2003; N.K. Singh Review Committee (2017): general government debt 60% of GDP (Centre 40%, States 20%), fiscal deficit 3% — UPSC 2018.
Escape clause lets the Centre deviate by up to 0.5% of GDP for national security, calamity, structural reforms or a sharp fall in output.
Recent anchor (as of 2025): Centre shifting from annual deficit targets to a debt-to-GDP path (~50% ± 1% by 2031); FY26 fiscal deficit target 4.4%.

nodes.title: Public Debt — Market Borrowing, Sovereign Debt & Sustainability
prelimsNote: Internal debt: dated securities (largest component, issued at market-related rates in auctions — UPSC 2022), T-bills, cash management bills; small savings via NSSF.
Art 292: Union borrows on the security of the Consolidated Fund within limits fixed by Parliament (no limit fixed so far); Art 293: a State indebted to the Centre needs its consent to borrow.
Bond prices and yields move inversely; yields rise with inflation expectations, higher government borrowing and rising global rates (UPSC 2021).
India's FAR (Fully Accessible Route) G-secs included in J.P. Morgan's GBI-EM index from June 2024.
Household financial savings partly flow into government borrowing (UPSC 2022).

nodes.title: Subsidies — Merit vs Non-Merit, Rationalisation & DBT
prelimsNote: Merit subsidies (education, health, nutrition) have large positive externalities; non-merit subsidies largely benefit private consumption.
Major subsidies: food (NFSA via FCI), fertiliser, petroleum (LPG); fertiliser: urea MRP fixed by government, P&K under Nutrient Based Subsidy since 2010 (UPSC 2020).
Direct Benefit Transfer launched 1 Jan 2013; JAM trinity (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile); PAHAL (DBTL) for LPG.
PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana: free foodgrains to NFSA beneficiaries extended for five years from 1 Jan 2024.
Trap: WTO Amber Box covers trade-distorting domestic support; India's food procurement is protected by the Peace Clause (Bali 2013).

nodes.title: Tax Reforms — GST, Direct Tax Code & Compliance
prelimsNote: 101st Amendment 2016; GST in force from 1 July 2017 — destination-based tax; Art 246A concurrent taxing power; IGST on inter-state supplies (Art 269A).
GST Council (Art 279A): Union FM chairs; Centre 1/3 vote weight, States 2/3; decisions by 3/4 of weighted votes; recommendations not binding (Mohit Minerals 2022).
Outside GST: alcohol for human consumption; petroleum crude, diesel, petrol, natural gas, ATF levied only from a date the Council recommends; electricity; stamp duty.
GST rationalisation (Sept 2025): mainly two slabs, 5% and 18%, plus 40% on demerit goods (as of late 2025).
Direct taxes: the Income-tax Act 2025 replaces the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026; earlier Direct Tax Code (2009/2010) was never enacted.
Traps: equalisation levy (2016) targeted digital ad services of non-residents (UPSC 2018); BEPS is an OECD/G20 project against tax avoidance by MNCs (UPSC 2016).

nodes.title: External Trade — FTP, WTO Obligations & Trade Disputes
prelimsNote: Foreign Trade Policy 2023 (from 1 April 2023) has no end date; target of $2 trillion exports by 2030.
RoDTEP replaced the WTO-incompatible MEIS; Districts as Export Hubs initiative.
India runs a merchandise trade deficit and a services surplus; overall current account usually in deficit (UPSC 2020).
Rupee trade settlement mechanism introduced by RBI in 2022.
WTO disputes: US–India solar DCR (2016), sugar subsidies (2021).

nodes.title: FDI — Policy, Sectoral Limits & Impact
prelimsNote: FDI policy is framed by DPIIT; FIPB abolished in 2017 — approvals now by ministries via the Foreign Investment Facilitation Portal.
Two routes: automatic and government approval.
Prohibited: atomic energy, lottery, gambling/betting, chit funds, Nidhi companies, real estate business/farm houses, TDR trading, tobacco manufacturing.
Press Note 3 (2020): investment from countries sharing a land border with India needs government approval.
FDI is a largely non-debt creating, long-term capital flow (UPSC 2020); FDI cap in insurance raised to 100% in Budget 2025.

nodes.title: Foreign Investment — FDI vs FPI, FIPB & Policy Changes
prelimsNote: FDI vs FPI: 10% or more of equity of a listed company = FDI; below 10% = FPI (Arvind Mayaram Committee).
Counted as FDI: equity in unlisted firms, 10%+ of listed firms, FCCBs and GDRs; NRE deposits are not FDI (UPSC 2012, 2021).
Participatory Notes (ODIs) are issued by registered FPIs to overseas investors not registered in India (UPSC 2019).
FIPB abolished in 2017.
FDI is non-debt creating and long-term; FPI is volatile 'hot money' (UPSC 2011, 2020).

nodes.title: New Economic Policy 1991 — LPG Reforms & Outcomes
prelimsNote: Industrial licensing abolished except a short list (now: alcoholic drinks, cigarettes, defence aerospace & equipment, industrial explosives, hazardous chemicals).
Industries reserved for the public sector cut from 17 to 8 in 1991; now only atomic energy and railway operations.
Rupee devalued in July 1991; LERMS 1992; current account convertibility in August 1994 (IMF Article VIII).
MRTP Act replaced by the Competition Act 2002 (Competition Commission of India).
Outcomes (UPSC 2016, 2020): agriculture's share in GDP fell, FDI inflows rose, services-led growth; share of India's exports in world trade rose only modestly.

nodes.title: Industrial Policy Evolution — IPR 1948, 1956, 1991 & NIP
prelimsNote: IPR 1948: mixed economy; IPR 1956 (Mahalanobis): Schedule A (17 industries exclusive to the State), B (12, progressively State-owned), C (private sector).
1970s–80s: focus on small-scale reservation, MRTP and FERA controls.
NIP 1991: de-licensing, de-reservation, automatic approval for FDI up to 51% in high-priority industries, removal of MRTP asset threshold.
National Manufacturing Policy 2011: NIMZs and 25% manufacturing share target.
Now reserved for the public sector: only atomic energy and railway operations.

nodes.title: Make in India — Manufacturing Ecosystem & Challenges
prelimsNote: Launched September 2014; goal of raising manufacturing to 25% of GDP; 25 sectors initially (27 in Make in India 2.0).
Production Linked Incentive schemes (2020–21) across 14 sectors — used by domestic and some foreign firms (UPSC 2023).
India's share of global merchandise exports is under 2% — the UPSC 2023 statement claiming 3.2% was false.
Domestic Content Requirement in solar (JNNSM) was challenged by the US at the WTO (UPSC 2017).
Supporting initiatives: Phased Manufacturing Programme (electronics), Semicon India Programme, PM Gati Shakti.

nodes.title: MSME Sector — Role, Problems & Policy Support
prelimsNote: MSMED Act 2006; composite definition (investment + turnover) since 2020; limits raised in Budget 2025 (micro ₹2.5 cr/₹10 cr; small ₹25 cr/₹100 cr; medium ₹125 cr/₹500 cr).
Trap: 'medium enterprises = ₹15–25 crore investment' is the old/false figure (UPSC 2023); all bank loans to MSMEs qualify as priority-sector lending.
Udyam registration (2020); CGTMSE credit guarantees; TReDS for receivables; MSME Samadhaan for delayed payments.
Sec 43B(h) of the Income-tax Act (2023): payments to micro & small suppliers must be made within 45 days to be deductible.
MSMEs contribute about 30% of GDP and roughly 45% of exports (approximate, as of 2024).

nodes.title: Special Economic Zones (SEZs) — Issues & Outcomes
prelimsNote: SEZ policy 2000; SEZ Act 2005; Board of Approval under the Ministry of Commerce.
SEZs are deemed foreign territory for trade operations, duties and tariffs; units must be net foreign-exchange earners.
Tax incentives eroded: MAT and DDT exemptions withdrawn (2011–12); income-tax holiday sunset for new units from 2020.
Kandla (1965) was Asia's first Export Processing Zone; Baba Kalyani Committee (2018) proposed the DESH framework.

nodes.title: Industrial Corridors & Manufacturing Hubs
prelimsNote: Delhi–Mumbai Industrial Corridor (Japan-assisted) was the first, along the Western Dedicated Freight Corridor.
National Industrial Corridor Development Programme — 11 corridors; 12 new industrial smart cities approved in August 2024.
Greenfield smart cities: Dholera (Gujarat), Shendra–Bidkin/AURIC (Maharashtra).
Dedicated Freight Corridors: Eastern (Ludhiana–Sonnagar) and Western (Dadri–JNPT).
PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan (Oct 2021): GIS-based multimodal infrastructure planning.

nodes.title: Ease of Doing Business — Reforms & India's Global Ranking
prelimsNote: World Bank's Doing Business report discontinued in 2021 after data irregularities; India rose to 63rd (2020) from 142nd (2014).

Sub-indices: starting a business, construction permits, getting electricity, registering property, getting credit, protecting minority investors, paying taxes, trading across borders, enforcing contracts, resolving insolvency.
Trap: 'maintenance of law and order' is NOT a sub-index (UPSC 2019).
Replaced by the World Bank's B-READY (Business Ready) report from 2024.
Domestic: DPIIT's Business Reform Action Plan ranks States; Jan Vishwas Act 2023 decriminalised 183 provisions.

nodes.title: Start-up Ecosystem — Funding, Policy & Angel Investment
prelimsNote: Startup India (Jan 2016): DPIIT recognition for entities up to 10 years old with turnover ≤ ₹100 crore.
Fund of Funds for Startups (₹10,000 crore) managed by SIDBI.
'Angel tax' (Sec 56(2)(viib)) abolished from FY 2025-26 (Budget 2024).
Unicorn = privately held start-up valued at ≥ US$1 billion.

nodes.title: Road & Highway Development — NHDP, Bharatmala
prelimsNote: NHDP (1998): Golden Quadrilateral (Delhi–Mumbai–Chennai–Kolkata) and North–South & East–West corridors.
Trap: the East–West corridor connects Silchar and Porbandar — not Dibrugarh and Surat (UPSC 2023).
Bharatmala Pariyojana (2017): economic corridors, inter-corridors, border and coastal roads; NHAI under the NHAI Act 1988.
National highways are on the Union List; PMGSY (2000) builds rural roads.
Financing: HAM, BOT-toll, TOT and NHAI InvITs.

nodes.title: Railway Reforms — Safety, Privatisation & High-Speed Rail
prelimsNote: Railways are on the Union List; Railway Budget merged with the Union Budget in 2017.
Railway operations remain reserved for the public sector (with atomic energy).
Mumbai–Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail with Japanese (Shinkansen) technology and JICA loan.
Kavach: indigenous automatic train protection system developed by RDSO.
Dedicated Freight Corridors and the National Rail Plan 2030 aim to raise rail's share in freight.

nodes.title: Port Development — Sagarmala & Maritime Logistics
prelimsNote: Major ports are under the Union; Major Port Authorities Act 2021 replaced the Major Port Trusts Act 1963.
Kamarajar Port: first major port registered as a company; Mundra: largest private port (UPSC 2023).
Trap: Visakhapatnam is NOT India's largest container port — JNPT (Nhava Sheva) is (UPSC 2023).
Sagarmala (2015): port modernisation, connectivity, port-led industrialisation, coastal community development.
Maritime India Vision 2030 and Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047; Vadhavan deep-draft port approved in 2024.

nodes.title: Civil Aviation — UDAN Scheme & Airport Development
prelimsNote: UDAN (2016) under the National Civil Aviation Policy 2016: regional connectivity with viability gap funding and capped fares.
Regulators: DGCA (safety), AERA (airport tariffs); AAI manages most airports.
India is the 3rd largest domestic aviation market.
GAGAN: satellite-based augmentation system built by ISRO and AAI.

nodes.title: Inland Waterways Development
prelimsNote: National Waterways Act 2016 declared 111 National Waterways (5 existing + 106 new); IWAI set up in 1986.
NW-1: Ganga–Bhagirathi–Hooghly (Haldia–Prayagraj), the longest; NW-2: Brahmaputra; NW-3: West Coast Canal.
Jal Marg Vikas Project (World Bank-assisted) on NW-1 with multimodal terminals at Varanasi, Sahibganj and Haldia.
Shipping and navigation on national waterways is a Union List subject.

nodes.title: Telecom Infrastructure — BharatNet, 5G & Digital Divide
prelimsNote: BharatNet (formerly NOFN, 2011): optical fibre to all gram panchayats, implemented by Bharat Broadband Nigam Ltd.
5G services launched in October 2022.
Telecommunications Act 2023 replaced the Indian Telegraph Act 1885; USOF renamed Digital Bharat Nidhi.
TRAI (TRAI Act 1997) regulates tariffs; appeals go to TDSAT.

nodes.title: Energy Infrastructure — Power Sector Reforms & Grid Management
prelimsNote: Electricity is on the Concurrent List; Electricity Act 2003; CERC and SERCs regulate tariffs.
One Nation One Grid achieved with synchronisation of the southern grid (2013); Green Energy Corridors for renewables.
UDAY (2015): States took over discom debt (UPSC 2016); RDSS (2021) for loss reduction and smart prepaid metering.
Non-fossil sources crossed 50% of installed capacity in 2025, ahead of the 2030 NDC target (as of 2025).
Electricity carries 19.85% weight in the Index of Eight Core Industries.

nodes.title: Public-Private Partnership — Models, Issues & Reforms
prelimsNote: Models: BOT (toll/annuity), BOOT, BOO, DBFOT, TOT, EPC (fully government-funded), Hybrid Annuity Model (government pays 40% during construction).
Swiss Challenge: an unsolicited proposal is opened for counter-bids, with the originator allowed to match.
Kelkar Committee (2015) on revisiting and revitalising PPPs.
Viability Gap Funding: up to 20% of project cost from the Centre (+ up to 20% from the sponsoring authority).

nodes.title: Investment Models — PPP, Viability Gap Funding, Hybrid Annuity
prelimsNote: National Infrastructure Pipeline (₹111 lakh crore, 2020–25); National Monetisation Pipeline (₹6 lakh crore, 2021) — brownfield assets, ownership retained by government.
NaBFID (2021): development finance institution for infrastructure; NIIF (2015): government-anchored investment fund (not an organ of NITI Aayog — UPSC 2017).
InvITs and REITs (SEBI, 2014) pool income-generating infrastructure/real-estate assets.
Interest income distributed by InvITs is taxable in investors' hands (UPSC 2023 tested InvIT taxation and their status under SARFAESI).
HAM (2016) balances risk between government and private developer in highways.

newNodesToCreate.title: Basic Economic Concepts — Opportunity Cost, Micro vs Macro & Externalities
prelimsNote: Opportunity cost = value of the next best alternative given up; free goods have no opportunity cost.
Change in a good's own price causes movement along the demand curve; income, tastes and prices of related goods shift the curve.
Giffen good: inferior good whose demand rises with price; Veblen good: prestige good demanded more when expensive.
Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable; externalities (positive/negative) justify Pigouvian taxes or subsidies.
Real sector = production of goods and services (farmers harvesting, mills making cloth) — not bank lending or bond issues (UPSC 2022).
For a firm, acquiring new technology is capital expenditure; debt vs equity financing is not 'capital vs revenue expenditure' (UPSC 2022).

newNodesToCreate.title: Inflation — CPI vs WPI, Headline vs Core, Phillips Curve & Base Effect
prelimsNote: CPI (NSO/MoSPI, base 2012) covers goods AND services, food weight ~46% in CPI-Combined; WPI (Office of Economic Adviser, DPIIT, base 2011-12) has no services (UPSC 2020).
RBI targets CPI-Combined headline inflation (4% ± 2%); core inflation excludes food and fuel.
Demand-pull (excess demand, monetised deficit — UPSC 2013) vs cost-push (input costs, supply shocks); stagflation = high inflation + stagnant output.
Phillips Curve: short-run inverse relation between inflation and unemployment; vertical in the long run at the natural rate/NAIRU (Friedman).
Base effect: a low (high) base last year inflates (deflates) this year's rate (UPSC 2011); disinflation = falling rate, deflation = falling price level.
Inflation benefits debtors and hurts creditors and fixed-income earners (UPSC 2013).

newNodesToCreate.title: Poverty & Inequality Measurement — Tendulkar, Rangarajan, MPI, Gini & Lorenz Curve
prelimsNote: Poverty committees: Alagh (1979, calorie norm 2400 rural/2100 urban), Lakdawala (1993), Tendulkar (2009; 21.9% poor in 2011-12), Rangarajan (2014; 29.5%).
State poverty lines differ because of differences in price levels (UPSC 2019).
Global MPI (UNDP + OPHI): 3 dimensions (health, education, standard of living), 10 indicators; NITI Aayog's national MPI uses 12 (adds maternal health and bank account).
Gini coefficient: 0 = perfect equality, 1 = perfect inequality; Lorenz curve farther from the 45° line means more inequality.
HDI (UNDP, concept by Mahbub ul Haq): life expectancy, education (mean & expected years of schooling), GNI per capita (PPP).
Global Hunger Index (Concern Worldwide & Welthungerhilfe): undernourishment, child stunting, child wasting, child mortality (UPSC 2016); Global Gender Gap Index by WEF (UPSC 2017).

newNodesToCreate.title: Human Development & Global Indices — Publishers and Indicators
prelimsNote: UNDP: HDI, MPI (with OPHI); WEF: Global Competitiveness Report, Global Gender Gap Index (UPSC 2017, 2019).
IMF: World Economic Outlook, Global Financial Stability Report (UPSC 2014, 2016); World Bank: World Development Report.
World Justice Project: Rule of Law Index (UPSC 2018); UNCTAD: World Investment Report.
Demographic dividend = growth boost from a rising working-age share; reaped through skills, health and jobs (UPSC 2013).
Trap: matching a report to the wrong publisher is UPSC's commonest one-liner trap in this area.

newNodesToCreate.title: Money Supply & RBI Instruments — M0–M4, Money Multiplier, CRR, SLR, Repo & OMO
prelimsNote: M0 = reserve/high-powered money; M1 = currency with public + demand deposits + other deposits with RBI; M3 (broad money) = M1 + time deposits; liquidity falls from M1 to M4 (UPSC 2013).
Money multiplier = broad money ÷ reserve money; it rises when the public holds less cash and banks hold fewer reserves (UPSC 2021).
Quantitative tools: CRR (no interest paid), SLR (cash, gold, approved securities), repo, SDF, MSF, Bank Rate, OMO; qualitative: margin requirements, moral suasion, selective credit control.
Expansionary policy: cut CRR/SLR/repo and buy G-secs via OMO (UPSC 2020); a lower SLR lets banks lend more (UPSC 2015).
Sterilisation: RBI offsets the liquidity impact of forex intervention through OMOs/MSS (UPSC 2023).
Higher demand for money with unchanged supply raises interest rates (UPSC 2013).

newNodesToCreate.title: Banking Structure & Regulation — Basel III, PSL, Co-operative, Payments & Small Finance Banks
prelimsNote: Basel III in India: minimum CRAR 9% (Basel: 8%) + 2.5% capital conservation buffer; CAR is prescribed by RBI, not decided by each bank (UPSC 2018).
Priority Sector Lending: 40% of ANBC for commercial banks; 75% for RRBs and Small Finance Banks.
Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act 2020 brought urban co-operative banks under RBI supervision; they can now issue equity/preference shares (UPSC 2021).
DICGC insures deposits up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank (since 2020).
On a bank's balance sheet, deposits are liabilities; advances, investments and money at call are assets (UPSC 2019).
RRBs (1975) are sponsored by commercial banks; Payments Banks cannot lend; SFBs must lend mainly to small borrowers.

newNodesToCreate.title: Money & Capital Markets — T-Bills, G-Secs, Bond Yields, P-Notes, Commercial Paper & SGB
prelimsNote: Money market (< 1 year): call/notice money, T-bills (91/182/364 days), Cash Management Bills, Commercial Paper (corporates, 7 days–1 year), Certificates of Deposit (banks).
Capital market: government bond market and stock market — call money and T-bill markets are NOT capital markets (UPSC 2023).
T-bills are issued only by the Government of India, at a discount to face value; States issue none (UPSC 2018).
Bond prices and yields move inversely; an inverted yield curve (short > long yields) signals recession risk.

Masala bonds: rupee-denominated bonds issued abroad (IFC first, 2014); Sovereign Gold Bonds issued by RBI for GoI (8-year tenor, exit after 5 years; new issues halted in 2024-25); Sovereign Green Bonds from 2023.
REITs/InvITs pool rental/toll-generating assets; credit rating agencies are regulated by SEBI (UPSC 2022).

newNodesToCreate.title: Tax Concepts — Direct vs Indirect, Progressive Taxation, Buoyancy, Cess & Surcharge
prelimsNote: Progressive tax: rate rises with income; regressive: burden falls more on the poor; proportional: same rate for all.
Tax buoyancy = responsiveness of revenue to GDP including discretionary changes; tax elasticity excludes policy changes.
Cess (Art 270) and surcharge (Art 271) are outside the divisible pool — not shared with States.
Tax incidence: a tax is shifted forward to consumers more when demand is inelastic relative to supply.
Indirect transfers: tax on transfer of foreign company shares deriving value from Indian assets (Vodafone; retrospective tax repealed 2021 — UPSC 2022).
A falling tax-GDP ratio can signal slowing growth or weaker tax effort (UPSC 2015, 2017).

newNodesToCreate.title: Balance of Payments (BoP) — Current vs Capital Account, CAD, Forex Reserves & REER/NEER
prelimsNote: Current account = trade in goods + invisibles (services, remittances, primary income); capital account = FDI, FPI, ECB, NRI deposits, loans.
A foreign tourist's spending in India is an export of services (UPSC 2011).
Forex reserves = Foreign Currency Assets (largest) + gold + SDRs + Reserve Tranche Position with IMF (UPSC 2013); import cover = months of imports reserves can finance.
Rupee fully convertible on current account since 1994; capital account partly — Tarapore Committees 1997 and 2006.
NEER rise = rupee appreciation; REER rise = loss of trade competitiveness; higher domestic inflation widens the NEER–REER gap (UPSC 2022).
Rupee depreciation: RBI sells dollars; Fed tightening causes capital flight and raises the cost of existing ECBs; devaluation increases ECB currency risk (UPSC 2022).

newNodesToCreate.title: Multilateral Financial Institutions & WTO — IMF, World Bank, SDR, WTO Boxes & Agreements
prelimsNote: IMF quotas determine voting power; SDR basket has 5 currencies — USD, EUR, CNY (added 2016 — UPSC 2016), JPY, GBP; Reserve/Gold Tranche drawings carry no conditionality (UPSC 2020).
World Bank Group: IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA, ICSID — India is not a member of ICSID.
WTO (1995): Amber Box (trade-distorting support; de minimis 10% for developing countries), Blue Box, Green Box; Peace Clause (Bali 2013) protects India's public stockholding.

TRIMS prohibit quantitative restrictions on imports by foreign investors, apply only to goods (not services) and do not regulate foreign investment as such (UPSC 2020); Trade Facilitation Agreement in force Feb 2017, ratified by India (UPSC 2017).
GI Act 1999 was enacted to meet TRIPS obligations (UPSC 2018).
AIIB: China largest, India second-largest shareholder, members include non-Asian countries (UPSC 2019); NDB headquartered in Shanghai (UPSC 2016).

newNodesToCreate.title: Industrial Indices — IIP & Index of Eight Core Industries
prelimsNote: IIP: base 2011-12, released monthly by NSO (MoSPI); manufacturing has the largest weight (~78%).
Index of Eight Core Industries: released by the Office of the Economic Adviser (DPIIT); ~40.27% weight in IIP.
Weights: Refinery Products 28.04 > Electricity 19.85 > Steel 17.92 > Coal 10.33 > Crude Oil 8.98 > Natural Gas 6.88 > Cement 5.37 > Fertilizers 2.63 (UPSC 2012, 2015).
Trap: fertilizers carry the lowest weight and refinery products the highest; IIP and the Core index are released by different agencies.
Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) by NSO is the main source of organised manufacturing statistics.

newNodesToCreate.title: Social Security, Insurance & Livelihood Schemes
prelimsNote: Atal Pension Yojana: ages 18–40, guaranteed pension ₹1,000–5,000 from 60; spouse gets the same pension, then corpus to nominee; not restricted to one member per family (UPSC 2016).
PMJJBY (₹2 lakh life cover, ages 18–50) and PMSBY (₹2 lakh accident cover, ages 18–70); PM-SYM gives unorganised workers ₹3,000/month pension with matching contribution.
PM MUDRA Yojana: Shishu (≤ ₹50,000), Kishore (₹50,000–5 lakh), Tarun (₹5–10 lakh), Tarun Plus (₹10–20 lakh, from 2024); Stand Up India: ₹10 lakh–1 crore for SC/ST and women, refinance via SIDBI.

MGNREGA: 100 days of wage employment per rural household per year, wages indexed to CPI-AL, at least one-third women. A 2025 law to replace it with a new rural employment guarantee — check current status.
NFSA 2013: 5 kg grain per person per month (35 kg for AAY households); eldest woman aged 18+ is head of household for ration cards (UPSC 2018).
PM SVANidhi (street vendors' collateral-free loans) and DAY-NRLM (SHG-based livelihoods) are other high-yield schemes.
